accroche: Between 1872 and 1876, a converted warship traveled 127580 km for the first systematic study of the world's oceans
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 7, 1872, HMS Challenger sails from Sheerness. She is a Royal Navy warship, a corvette, but almost all her guns have been removed to make room for laboratories, sounding winches, and storage rooms for specimens. On board is a scientific team led by Charles Wyville Thomson, professor of natural history at the University of Edinburgh, who will describe this conviction, already old by 1868, at the time of the Lightning dredgings, in the book he publishes in 1873: "I had long previously had a profound conviction that the land of promise for the naturalist […] was the bottom of the deep sea," the ocean floor as the naturalist's last promised land. For three and a half years, the ship will try to test this conviction, systematically.

## A Method Rather Than an Adventure

At each of the 362 stations where the Challenger stops, the team repeats the same protocol: sounding the depth, taking the temperature at different levels, dredging the bottom to bring up the organisms living there, analyzing the water. This is not a voyage of exploration in the romantic sense of the term. It is the first methodical and systematic application of scientific measurement to all the world's oceans. On March 23, 1875, at station 225, in the Pacific, a sounding reaches 4475 fathoms, or about 8184 meters, the greatest depth ever measured until then, in an area that will later be identified as the Mariana Trench. Later, more precise soundings will show that the deepest point of the trench lies even lower; the Challenger did not find the absolute bottom of the ocean, but it proved that one could go looking for it.

## What the Voyage Refuted

The most significant result is not the depth record. It is what came up from the bottom. The National Oceanography Centre, which today holds the expedition's archives, puts it plainly: the team collected and cataloged more than 4700 new marine species, which proved that life exists under extreme pressure and in the total darkness of the deep sea, contradicting the idea, widespread in the mid-19th century, that the deep ocean would be too hostile to harbor any form of life.

The Challenger returns to Spithead on May 24, 1876, after 68890 nautical miles, or about 127580 kilometers. But the voyage does not end there: the synthesis of the data collected, the *Challenger Report*, runs to fifty volumes and is not completed until 1895, under the direction of the naturalist John Murray after Thomson's death in 1882. It is this body of work, more than the voyage itself, that tips the study of the oceans from a collectors' curiosity into an organized science, with its own methods and its own questions. It is the birth certificate of modern oceanography.

quiz.question: What did the HMS Challenger expedition (1872-1876) establish, contrary to a received idea of the time?
choix: That the Earth is older than 19th-century geologists thought
That deep ocean currents flow faster than surface currents
That life exists in the total darkness and extreme pressure of the deep sea
That the Mariana Trench is the deepest point of all the world's oceans
quiz.explication: The 4700 new species brought up by dredging proved that abundant life exists in total darkness and under extreme pressure, contradicting the widespread idea that the deep sea would be too hostile to any life. The Challenger's record sounding was not at the deepest point known today: later, more precise measurements showed that the Mariana Trench goes down even lower.
